temp_bound: one deterministic '<target>.tmp' per target; removed on every exit path; a kill leaves at most that one file; each owner sweeps '<target>.tmp' and legacy '<target>[.<pid>].<32hex>.tmp' / '.<target>...' siblings at construction, before its first write; only exact-name siblings match, never the target or other targets

chain_removal.signal: No event type reliably ends a journey: a duplicate/redelivered signal re-enters the same journey (paper_order_simulated noop) while its 30-day execution decision exists, and test_lifecycle_outbox_ambiguous_send_replays_exact_payloads_and_chain proves a chain must continue after a fill. A chain is therefore removed only when the journey has nothing pending AND its last event_time is older than PANTHEON_LIFECYCLE_CHAIN_RETENTION_SECONDS (default 35 days > 30 day decision TTL).
chain_removal.open_journeys: journeys with pending events or events inside the window keep their exact sequence_no/causal checkpoint (unit-tested)

growth_bound: outbox bytes ~= (journeys in the 35-day window) x ~0.6 KB checkpoint + pending; tested on 20000 chains (15000 older than window -> 15000 removed, 5000 kept)
write_cost: Full-file rewrite per admit/ack is NOT removed; the cost is bounded by pruning the file to the window instead of growing forever. Not measured on a real 41 MB file.
retired_binding_cleanup: reconciler _cleanup_retired_state_files: only status=retired bindings reported by the runtime-manager, not desired, no live worker, ledger pending_fill_publications/pending_performance_pair empty and outbox pending empty; unreadable files are kept; removes state, outbox, member-books, locks and temps
rollback: No persisted schema change: same keys, same file names; the previous release reads state files unchanged and ignores the (now absent) pruned chains; legacy tmp names are not read by anyone.

residual_findings: Hosted-shape one-time cleanup (156 outbox files, 563 orphan tmp = 4.85 GB) is by design on first start / retirement; not run against the real host in this task.

Member-books file is persona-scoped and may be shared by concurrent runtimes across a replacement; the deterministic temp name can collide for two simultaneous writers and a startup sweep may delete a peer's in-flight temp (previously random names).
